name: Rhodiola rosea

lead: Rhodiola rosea is an Arctic and mountain succulent whose root is sold as an adaptogen for stress, fatigue and stamina. People use it to stay energised and recover, which supports more consistent training and a fitter, fresher appearance.

Its rosavins and salidroside are reported in cell and animal studies to have antioxidant, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory activity. A 2010 review summarised its clinical efficacy, while a 2012 European Medicines Agency report described the published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. Some forum posts discuss hormone effects, but no study cited tests that.

paras: It is taken as a standardised root extract in capsules, usually in the morning around work or training. Users generally report noticing effects on fatigue over days to a few weeks, and combine it with other adaptogens and sleep and recovery habits.

FDA has issued warning letters over unapproved health claims. The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II because wild populations are overharvested, and products can be adulterated. Human adverse effects are not well covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Rhodiola is taken as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue: less fatigue means better energy and training capacity, which supports a fitter, fresher look. Human trials on fatigue vary in quality.

lead: Rhodiola rosea, called golden root, rose root or Arctic root, is a perennial succulent of the stonecrop family that grows in cold, mountainous and Arctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America. Its rhizome is sold as an adaptogen, a supplement category marketed for stress, fatigue and stamina[1][2]. In appearance terms, people who take it describe a chain rather than a direct effect: steadier energy and stress tolerance, more consistent training and sleep, and from there a better physique, skin and overall look[3][4].

The rhizome holds roughly 140 compounds, including the phenylpropanoids rosavin, rosarin and rosin and the phenylethanoid salidroside[1][5]. Research on the plant spans laboratory work on salidroside in cells and animals[6][7][8][9][10], reviews of its traditional use and chemistry[5], and human trials that have mostly examined mental fatigue, stress, mood and exercise performance[3][4][11][12][13].

Reviewers differ in how they read that literature. A 2022 review in Molecules described the clinical findings on stress-related symptoms as encouraging[3], and a 2024 review in the British Journal of Nutrition found that acute supplementation may prolong time to exhaustion in recreationally active adults while effects of chronic use are less documented[4]. Wikipedia cites a 2012 European Medicines Agency report concluding that the published trials had considerable quality deficiencies and that well-established use could not be accepted[1]. Within looksmaxxing forums the plant appears occasionally, in threads about productivity supplements and questions about hormones[14].

paras: The plant grows 5 to 40 cm tall, with fleshy stems rising from a short scaly rootstock and yellow to greenish-yellow flowers in summer. It is dioecious, with separate male and female plants[1]. It grows on sea cliffs and at altitude across much of the Arctic, the mountains of Central Asia and Europe, and parts of eastern North America; some North American plants once placed in the species are now classified as R. integrifolia and R. rhodantha[1].

Leaves and shoots are reported to be edible raw or cooked, with a bitter taste, and an extract is sometimes used to flavour vodka[1]. The root is the part used in supplements and traditional preparations.

Pedanius Dioscorides described the plant in De Materia Medica, and Carl Linnaeus later gave it its binomial name[1]. It is used in traditional medicine in Asia and Eastern Europe, where it is sold as capsules, liquid extracts and tablets[1]. The 2010 Phytomedicine review covers its traditional use in Scandinavia, Russia and Asia, where it was taken to stimulate the nervous system, ease fatigue and build physical performance[5][3].

The idea that rhodiola is an adaptogen comes from Soviet-era research. Toxicologist Nikolai Lazarev coined the word in 1947 for substances thought to raise resistance to stress[2]. A 2021 historical review in Nutrients states that plant adaptogens, including Rhodiola rosea, were first used in professional sports about 50 years before its publication for their potential to increase resistance to stress and improve endurance[15]. A 1999 paper grouped related herbs under the adaptogen label in Ayurvedic medicine[16]. Wikipedia notes that adaptogen is not an approved marketing term in the EU or US and that the EMA has said the term is not accepted in mainstream pharmacological practice, while critics describe the definition as vague[2].

Roots and rhizomes contain monoterpene alcohols and glycosides, cyanogenic glycosides, aryl glycosides, phenylethanoids, phenylpropanoids, flavonoids, flavonolignans, proanthocyanidins and gallic acid derivatives[5]. Concentrations of rosavin, rosarin and rosin vary with origin and are reported highest in Russian-origin plants[1]. Wikipedia states that no physiological effect of rosavin, rosarin, rosin or salidroside has been demonstrated in humans[1].

Studies on isolated organs, cells and enzymes have reported neuroprotective, cardioprotective, anti-fatigue, antidepressive, anxiolytic and nootropic activity for rhodiola preparations, with several candidate mechanisms[5]. Salidroside protected human neuroblastoma cells against oxidative and amyloid-induced injury in laboratory studies[6][7], stimulated the Sirt1/PGC-1 alpha axis in a mouse diabetic-nephropathy model[8], and reduced inflammatory signalling in psoriasis-related and endothelial cell models[9][10]. A 2020 review collected research on anti-inflammatory effects of the extract and its compounds[17]. Another cell study reported apoptosis and autophagy in gastric cancer cells[18]. These are laboratory findings, not human outcomes.

For exercise, the 2024 British Journal of Nutrition review proposes, from rodent studies, modulation of energy substrate use, reduced fatigue and muscle damage, and altered antioxidant activity as possible routes[4].

Rhodiola is not marketed as a cosmetic. People who take it describe using it to manage stress and energy so that training, study or work routines hold up. In that chain, the appearance benefit is indirect: better recovery and consistency feed into muscle, body composition, sleep and skin. A looksmax.org poster asked whether it was safe to take for productivity while looksmaxxing, which shows the supplement being considered within an appearance-improvement routine[14].

A US homeopathic-style product label lists rhodiola among ingredients for an adrenal and DHEA formula whose stated indications include low energy and dry skin and hair, an example of how it is sometimes folded into appearance-adjacent wellness products[19].

Stress and fatigue. A double-blind crossover study of the standardised extract SHR-5 in 56 young healthy physicians measured mental performance on a fatigue index during night duty[11]. A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled parallel-group study of SHR-5 enrolled people with stress-related fatigue[12]. The 2010 review summarised such trials as showing an anti-fatigue effect on mental performance and reduced burnout in fatigue syndrome, with encouraging results for mild to moderate depression and generalised anxiety[5]; a 2011 review of herbal medicines for depression, anxiety and insomnia also examined rhodiola[20]. A 2022 review concentrated on life-stress symptoms and described the clinical evidence as encouraging[3].

Anxiety and mood. A randomised trial in 80 mildly anxious participants compared an extract with a no-treatment control over 14 days across four testing sessions, using self-report measures and cognitive tests[13].

Exercise. The 2024 review identified at least sixteen human investigations. It reports that acute supplementation before exercise may prolong time to exhaustion and improve time-trial performance in recreationally active adults, that chronic supplementation has limited documented benefit, that trials with higher intakes showed effects in sprint and resistance training, and that effects on muscle damage, inflammation, antioxidant activity and perceived exertion are equivocal[4]. A 2024 exploratory randomised trial examined salidroside and exercise performance in healthy active young adults[21].

Other studies. Registered trials have examined Rhodiola crenulata in COPD (57 participants) and in acute mountain sickness (125)[22][23], adults with ADHD (two Phase 4 studies of 60 each)[24][25], mental and physical fatigue (90)[26], and small exercise and cognition studies in resistance-trained adults, footballers and others (24 to 27 participants)[27][28][29]. A triple-blinded placebo-controlled study asked whether supplementation affects digital eye strain[30], and a 2026 randomised trial tested a protein supplement combining ashwagandha and rhodiola on sleep quality[31]. No trial has used a cosmetic or appearance measure.

Overall reading. Wikipedia reports that, through 2019, human studies lacked sufficient quality to show whether the plant affects fatigue or any other condition, and cites the 2012 EMA conclusion on trial quality[1]. A 2021 adaptogen review said human clinical trials of plant adaptogens remain limited while meta-analytic data pointed to benefits in chronic fatigue, cognitive impairment and immune protection[15].

The US FDA has issued warning letters to supplement makers over unapproved claims that rhodiola treats Raynaud syndrome, altitude sickness, depression and cancer, and over missing evidence of safety or efficacy[1]. More broadly, FDA letters between 2020 and 2023 targeted unapproved health claims on adaptogen-type supplements[2]. The EMA concluded in 2012 that well-established use could not be accepted[1].

Rhodiola is listed under CITES Appendix II. Demand is growing and supply comes largely from wild harvesting; with weak regulation this has led to environmental degradation, substitution or adulteration of products and illegal harvesting in protected areas. Some farmers and researchers see it as a possible cash crop in Arctic climates[1]. Product labels for rhodiola-containing formulas advise consulting a health professional during pregnancy or breastfeeding and if symptoms persist[19].

Rhodiola is a minor topic. The main thread found concerns a poster who had read online that it affects estrogen and testosterone and asked whether it could harm their looksmaxxing given an existing hormonal imbalance; a reply compared such supplements to energy drinks and advised avoiding them[14]. Hormone-focused human studies of rhodiola are not cited in the major reviews summarised above[5][3][4].
